subject: computer-science
title: Theory of Computation: Turing and FSMs
welcome_lead: Meet the abstract machines at the heart of computer science.
meta_desc: A-Level CS: Turing machines, finite state machines and what they can compute.
final_note: These models define the limits of what any computer can do.

concepts.def: An abstract model with an infinite tape that can simulate any algorithm.
A model with a finite set of states and transitions on input.
A Turing machine that can simulate any other Turing machine.
Anything effectively computable can be computed by a Turing machine.
A condition of a machine determining its response to input.
A rule moving the machine from one state to another on input.

walkthroughs.body_html: Alan Turing's 1936 machine has an infinite tape, a read/write head and a finite control. Despite its simplicity, it can compute anything any modern computer can — the Church-Turing thesis formalises this idea.

An FSM has finitely many states and transitions but no memory beyond the current state. They model traffic lights, vending machines and lexers — they cannot count arbitrarily but they are fast and easy to verify.

FSMs recognise regular languages. Push-down automata (FSM + stack) recognise context-free languages. Turing machines recognise everything computable — but cannot answer every question (see the halting problem).
